response.text:
I can’t view the file — I’m working only from your description. Based on that, here are focused layout changes I’d suggest and why, so you can decide before rendering.

1) Rebalance the composition
- Change: move the photo stack slightly toward center or overlap the two photos (staggered) instead of a strict left column.
- Why: a strict left stack with a headline across the top tends to leave the center visually empty and makes the poster feel left‑heavy. Bringing imagery toward the center creates a stronger focal area and smoother eye flow.

2) Clarify and strengthen hierarchy
- Change: make the headline the clear primary element (bigger, heavier weight), add a short subhead directly under it (1 line), and place a concise CTA near the QR code.
- Why: people scan posters quickly — a bold headline, one-line support, and a clear CTA guide attention and increase conversion.

3) Move and treat the QR code for better scanning and conversion
- Change: place the QR code adjacent to a short CTA (“Scan to apply” or “Learn more”), give it a white or light quiet zone/background, increase its size, and avoid tucking it in the absolute corner.
- Why: scanning reliability and click-through increase when the QR is prominent, has contrast/quiet zone, and is paired with explicit instructions.

4) Improve contrast and legibility on a dark background
- Change: add a semi-opaque overlay behind text (or use a lighter band) and choose high-contrast type colors; increase headline/subhead sizes for viewing distance.
- Why: dark backgrounds can make text hard to read; overlays preserve mood while ensuring legibility.

5) Unify photo treatment
- Change: match color grading, crop tight to faces/action, and use the same border style (round or subtle drop shadow).
- Why: consistent photo treatment reads as a single visual system and strengthens brand/credibility.

6) Create a visual path to the CTA
- Change: use alignment, a subtle diagonal or leading lines from photos → headline → QR/CTA, or color accent (single bright color) to pull the eye.
- Why: directing the eye intentionally increases the chance viewers reach and act on the QR/CTA.

7) Add minimal supporting copy and branding
- Change: include a one- or two-line benefit statement near the headline and place the logo where it balances the photos (top-left or bottom-left).
- Why: a short benefit tells viewers why to care; logo placement anchors brand without competing with the CTA.

8) Accessibility and production checks
- Change: ensure sufficient contrast ratios, avoid tiny all‑caps text, and make the QR large enough for expected viewing distance (don’t rely on tiny corner codes).
- Why: accessibility broadens reach and prevents scanning/legibility failures in print or photos of the poster.

Quick alternatives if you want different feels:
- High-impact: replace the two stacked photos with one large hero photo at left or full-bleed and lay headline over the image with a dark text band.
- Clean/minimal: reduce to one cropped portrait, headline top-left, CTA center-bottom above a larger QR in the lower-right with a clear label.

Tell me which direction you prefer (conservative tweak, high-impact swap, or minimalist), and I’ll list exact type sizes, spacing, and a brief mockup plan before you render.
